assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Immobilized enzyme
items.clue: An enzyme held in a fixed position, for example by being embedded in a membrane.

items.label: Enzyme-substrate specificity
items.clue: The property that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or one type of reaction.

items.label: Enzyme-substrate complex
items.clue: The temporary structure formed while a substrate is bound to the active site of an enzyme.

items.label: Induced fit
items.clue: The model of enzyme-substrate binding in which the active site is not a rigid shape that exactly matches the substrate.

questions.stem: ATP synthase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and cannot move freely. How do its substrates, ADP and phosphate, reach its active site?

options.text: They move by random molecular motion in the fluid and collide with the fixed active site.
They cannot, so an enzyme fixed in a membrane works only after being released from it.
The enzyme extends its active site out into the fluid to capture passing substrates.
They are carried to the enzyme by a directed flow of fluid in the mitochondrion.

questions.stem: Lipase catalyses the hydrolysis of triglycerides but has no effect on starch. What is the reason?

options.text: Starch molecules are too large to enter the active site, but any molecule smaller than starch could.
The active site of lipase is complementary in shape and chemical properties to a triglyceride only.
Starch requires more energy to break down than lipase is able to supply to the reaction.
Lipase seeks out triglyceride molecules in the fluid and ignores starch molecules it meets.

questions.stem: At high substrate concentrations, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction levels off even when more substrate is added. Why?

options.text: Every active site is occupied almost all the time, so extra substrate finds no free site to bind.
The enzyme molecules have been used up by the reaction, so no more product can be formed.
The high concentration of substrate denatures the enzyme, so its active site stops working.
The amount of energy the enzyme can supply each second has reached its upper limit.

questions.stem: Illustrative data. Catalase was added to hydrogen peroxide and the volume of oxygen collected was recorded: 0 s, 0 cm³; 20 s, 12 cm³; 40 s, 20 cm³; 60 s, 24 cm³. What is the initial rate of reaction?

options.text: 0.40 cm³ s⁻¹
1.7 s per cm³
20 cm³ in 40 s
0.6 cm³ s⁻¹

questions.explanation: The initial rate is the gradient of the first, steepest part of the graph: 12 cm³ of oxygen in the first 20 s gives 12 / 20 = 0.6 cm³ s⁻¹.

questions.stem: How does an enzyme affect the energy changes of the reaction it catalyses?

options.text: It lowers the energy of the products, so that more energy is released overall than would be without the enzyme.
It lowers the activation energy but leaves the energy difference between substrate and products unchanged.
It supplies the activation energy, transferring its own energy to the substrate to break the bonds.
It releases energy by breaking bonds in the substrate, and this provides the activation energy.

questions.stem: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?

options.text: Its peptide bonds are broken, so the polypeptide chain splits into its separate amino acids.
Its shape alters only briefly and then returns to normal once the conditions are restored.
Its three-dimensional structure changes, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.
It is killed, because enzymes are living particles that are destroyed by heat or acid.

questions.stem: Which statement about intracellular and extracellular enzyme-catalysed reactions is correct?

options.text: Digestion in the gut is intracellular, because food is broken down inside the cells that line it.
The Krebs cycle is extracellular, because it breaks down food in the gut to release its energy.
Extracellular enzymes such as pepsin are made outside cells, which is why they act outside them.
Glycolysis is intracellular; chemical digestion in the gut is extracellular.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the Calvin cycle and the Krebs cycle from glycolysis?

options.text: The cycles regenerate all of their intermediates and so produce no net product, whereas glycolysis produces pyruvate as its end product.
In the cycles an intermediate used in the first step is regenerated in the last, whereas glycolysis runs from glucose to pyruvate in a chain.
The cycles use up their starting compound on every turn, so it must be supplied continuously from outside, unlike the glucose used in glycolysis.
The cycles take place in the gut, where food is broken down to release its energy, whereas glycolysis takes place inside cells.

questions.stem: Which statement about non-competitive inhibition at an allosteric site is correct?

options.text: The inhibitor binds permanently to the allosteric site, so the enzyme is inactivated for the rest of its life.
Any molecule of a suitable size can occupy the allosteric site, and it denatures the enzyme when it does so.
The inhibitor binds reversibly away from the active site, and the resulting shape change stops catalysis.
The inhibitor occupies the active site, and adding more substrate displaces it and restores the rate.

questions.stem: Statins are drugs prescribed to reduce blood cholesterol. How do they act?

options.text: They resemble the substrate of an enzyme in the cholesterol synthesis pathway and bind reversibly to its active site.
They hydrolyse cholesterol molecules that are already circulating in the blood into products that are excreted.
They bind permanently to the active site of the enzyme, so cholesterol synthesis stops for the rest of life.
They denature the cholesterol-synthesizing enzyme so that it can no longer fold into its working shape.
